title: Service Capacity Governance and Error Budget Handbook
author: Linh Tran
body:
Overview

Purpose
This handbook defines a standardized approach for service capacity planning, SLO and error budget governance, operational tooling, and runbook guidance for Redwood Inference services. It is intended for SREs, service owners, platform engineers, and incident commanders.

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference endpoints (hosted API, dedicated pools) and critical internal control-plane services that directly affect request success or latency.
- Does not replace product capacity plans for non-inference workloads (billing, analytics) but includes cross-team coordination expectations.

Who should read this
- Service owners and product managers responsible for traffic-bearing APIs
- SREs on-call for inference, routing, and autoscaling services
- Capacity planners and finance for reserved capacity procurement

Key definitions
- SLO (Service Level Objective): measurable SLA we aim to meet with a defined measurement window.
- Error budget: 1 - SLO measured over the SLO window. Burn indicates consumption of the budget.
- SLO window: rolling 28-day window unless otherwise specified.
- Critical service: services with error budgets shared by customer-facing inference calls.

SLO taxonomy and examples
- Availability SLO (success rate): % of inference requests returning 200-series responses within the service timeout. Default: 99.95% over 28d for hosted inference; 99.9% for Dedicated-tier customer-facing endpoints with SLA.
- Latency SLOs (p95/p99): p95 generation latency <= 250 ms for short-context endpoints (< 512 tokens) and p95 <= 600 ms for long-context endpoints (> 2048 tokens); p99 targets are guidance only and used for capacity planning.
- Throughput SLO: sustained request throughput with <= 5% increase in 95th-percentile latency compared to baseline under supported burst.

Error budget policy
1. Tracking
   - Error budget is calculated daily and shown in the SRE dashboard. Burn rate uses 28d rolling window.
   - Dashboard must show 28d consumed %, 7d trend, and last incident contribution.
2. Thresholds and actions
   - Green: <= 25% used — normal ops.
   - Watch: 25% < used <= 50% — reduce non-critical releases, notify product owners.
   - Elevated: 50% < used <= 80% — pause disruptive deployments, prioritize mitigations.
   - Critical: > 80% used — enact emergency capacity playbook (see section below), allocate runbook responders, and schedule post-incident review.
3. Deployment controls tied to error budget
   - CI gating: If error budget in any critical service is > 50% consumed, CI merges that change any dependent infra must be approved by SRE lead and feature owner.
   - Canary policy: Canary size must be reduced to <= 5% of traffic when entering Elevated state.

Capacity planning lifecycle (quarterly cadence)
- Inputs
  - Historical traffic (90/99 percentile daily patterns) and week-over-week growth projections from product telemetry.
  - Model change plans (new model sizes, quantization changes) from research/model-onboarding.
  - Committed Dedicated capacity contracts (sales/finance inputs).
  - Planned marketing events and known spikes (product calendar).
- Outputs
  - Capacity runbook: target GPU pool sizes, safety buffer (typically 30% for hosted during rolling deploys), planned procurement requests, and autoscale thresholds.
  - Thresholds for alerting and pre-warm scripts for expected events.
- Process steps (quarterly)
  1. Collect telemetry: p95/p99 latency, request rate, GPU utilization, avg tokens per request, and KV cache hit rate for the quarter.
  2. Forecast baseline growth conservatively: use both linear and 95th percentile modeling; present low/med/high scenarios.
  3. Translate forecast to GPU hours/capacity: include warmup and buffer for model rollouts.
  4. Produce purchase and reservation plan: recommend Dedicated reservations or cloud scale goals.
  5. Review with finance and product; publish capacity runbook and action items.

Operational scaling policies (run-time)
- Autoscaling rules (high level)
  - Primary signal: GPU utilization at 95th percentile over 5m. Target utilization 70%-80% for mixed-size pools.
  - Secondary signals: queue length, request latency, and batch fill rate.
  - Scale-up: triggered when 95thpt GPU util > 85% for 3 consecutive 1m evaluation windows or queue depth > configured threshold for 2m.
  - Scale-down: only performed when utilization < 40% for 15m and there is no ongoing rollout. Minimum pool size enforced per customer SLA.

- Prefill and prewarm policy for known events
  - For planned events > 10% traffic delta, prewarm pools 6 hours prior and run synthetic warmup to populate KV cache.

Incident response and error budget emergency playbook
1. Immediate triage (first 15 mins)
   - IC or on-call: declare P0 if > 50% global error budget burn or customer impact to > 10% customers.
   - Run initial checks: ingestion pipelines, redis/KV cache health, model runner errors, and autoscaling activity.
   - Post channel: #incidents and create incident in PagerDuty/Statuspage.
2. Containment (15–60 mins)
   - Enforce temporary rate-limits / degrade non-essential features (e.g., background embeddings).
   - Route traffic to lower-latency regions or fallback model variants if routing available.
   - If capacity shortage suspected: increase pool size (hot-path) and disable non-critical batch jobs.
3. Mitigation (1–6 hours)
   - Apply config rollbacks, model pins, or kernel fallback options.
   - If a code-related rollout caused burning, rollback canary to previous revision and reduce canary size.
4. Communication and escalation
   - Notify customer success and account owners if impact crosses SLA thresholds.
   - Exec summary to be posted in the incident doc within 4 hours.

Incident review standards (postmortem expectations)
- Every SEV ≥ P1 incident must have a postmortem within 72 hours. Postmortem must include:
  - Timeline with timestamps, contributing factors, root cause analysis, and a quantitative impact (error budget consumed, customer minutes lost).
  - Action items with owners and completion dates (must include at least one change to prevent recurrence).
  - Verification plan and regression tests to be added to CI/QA.
- Postmortem structure
  1. Summary and impact
  2. Timeline
  3. Root cause and contributing factors
  4. Remediation and follow-ups (with owners)
  5. Validation plan
  6. Retro notes and lessons learned

Operational tooling and dashboards
- SRE dashboard requirements (must exist for each critical service)
  - 28d rolling SLO indicator, 7d trend, incident burn table, and current burn rate.
  - Heatmap of request rate by model, region, and customer segment.
  - Autoscaler telemetry: scale events, decisions, and cooldowns.
  - Capacity view: GPU pool fill, reserved vs burst usage, and pending prewarm jobs.
- Must-have alerts
  - SLO breach predicted: forecasted burn rate projecting breach in < 24h.
  - Rapid burn spike: > 20% of budget consumed within 6h.
  - Autoscale saturation: >95% GPU util without scale-up for >3m.
  - Queue growth: sustained queue depth increase 2x baseline for 5m.

Runbook snippets (copyable commands and checks)
- Quick health checks
  - curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?model=short-context
  - kubectl get hpa -n inference --selector=pool=hosted
  - redis-cli -h kv-host INFO | grep used_memory_human
- Scale pool (example CLI)
  - rwoodctl pool scale --pool hosted-gpu-a100 --replicas 10 --priority prewarm
- Rollback canary
  - rwoodctl rollout rollback --service inference-api --revision previous --canary-size 2

Service ownership and escalation matrix
- On-call SRE: first responder for operational alerts (owned by SRE rotations).
- Service Owner: responsible for feature rollouts, capacity budget signoff, and customer communications.
- Platform Capacity Lead: approves reserved purchases and cross-service reallocation.
- PagerDuty escalation levels defined in the team wiki and must be included in runbook header.

Runbook template (required fields for every service runbook)
- Service name
- Primary contact and on-call rota link
- SLOs and error budget status link
- Critical thresholds and alerts list
- Quick diagnostics (commands)
- Emergency mitigation steps (top 5)
- Post-incident action owner and timeline

Regular exercises and reliability initiatives
- Quarterly game-days: simulate capacity loss, regional network partition, and model rollout regressions. Document findings and update capacity runbooks.
- Annual chaos experiments for dedicated pools and autoscaler logic with safety fences.
- Reliability improvement backlog: prioritized from postmortems and SLO breach root causes.

Auditable controls and review cadence
- Monthly: SRE lead reviews error budget status across critical services and flags at-risk services.
- Quarterly: Capacity planning review with product, finance, and platform.
- After each P1/P0 incident: mandatory postmortem review and remediation tracking until closure.

Appendices
A. Example SLO calculation (availability)
- Measurement: count(successful_requests) / count(total_requests) over a rolling 28-day window.
- Example: If 28d_total = 10,000,000 and 28d_failures = 5,000 => availability = 1 - 5,000/10,000,000 = 99.95%

B. Example capacity worksheet columns (CSV)
- date,avg_rps,p95_latency_ms,avg_tokens,kv_cache_hit,est_gpu_hours,buffer_pct,notes

C. Change log
